question: The European Court of Auditors (ECA) has identified significant shortcomings in the control of the recovery fund1, specifically, that information on final recipients, contractors, subcontractors, actual costs and results achieved is insufficient. Payments are also made on the basis of milestones and targets rather than actual costs.

This makes it difficult to assess whether taxpayers’ money has been used efficiently or whether Member States have been able to retain savings when measures turned out to be cheaper than estimated2. Given that the Recovery and Resilience Facility may be the model for future EU spending: 1.
How does the Commission intend to ensure value for money and that the use of taxpayers’ money has not resulted in overfunding, inefficient expenditure or savings that have not been reallocated?

Why does the Commission not systematically request actual cost data per measure when such data is necessary to assess efficiency, especially given that 70 % of Member States already collect this data systematically, which would allow the Commission to benchmark the cost of comparable measures across Member States?
Will the Commission guarantee that future EU instruments will come with binding requirements on full traceability, actual costs and public transparency, the best practices identified by the ECA?

European Court of Auditors’ Special Report 14/2026 on transparency and traceability in the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), https://www.eca.europa.eu/sv/publications/SR-2026-14. 2 The ECA found that for 15 out of 19 completed measures examined in four Member States, actual costs were lower than estimated, in some cases by up to 25 %. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) Regulation1 precludes the Commission from controlling the actual costs incurred by the Member States2. While the Commission has no legal mandate to systematically request information on actual costs, Member States can submit actual cost data when revising their Recovery and Resilience Plans (RRPs).

In such situations the Commission duly considers this data and requests clarifications when needed. Where the Commission has been informed of major cost savings under a specific measure, it has requested the respective Member State to address this when revising its RRP.
In this context, it should be noted that in its report, the European Court of Auditors has not identified deficiencies in the Commission’s application of the binding RRF legislative framework.

The principle of efficiency, among the principles of sound financial management under the Financial Regulation3, requires the best relationship between the resources employed, the activities undertaken and the achievement of objectives.

Accordingly, the efficiency of the RRF must be assessed by comparing the payments to the Member States against the achievement of the relevant milestones and targets, and the underlying reforms and investments, as set out and approved by the Council. The recast Financial Regulation4 (adopted in September 2024) widens the scope of the data collection and transparency requirements at EU level.

Furthermore, under the Commission’s proposal for future National and Regional Partnership Plans5, information on beneficiaries, recipients, final recipients, contractors and sub-contractors, including the amount of the EU contribution committed, as well as operations, will be collected and published.
1 Regulation (EU) 2021/241 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 February 2021 establishing the

Recovery and Resilience Facility, OJ L 57, 18.2.2021, pp. 17–75, http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/241/oj. 2 Recital 18 of the RRF Regulation. 3 https://commission.europa.eu/publications/eu-financial-regulation_en. 4 See footnote 3. 5 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52025PC0565.
